claims.text: There is a U-shaped association between the percentage of energy consumed from carbohydrate and overall mortality in the ARIC cohort.
Consuming 50-55% of energy from carbohydrates is associated with the lowest risk of mortality in the ARIC cohort.
Low carbohydrate consumption (<40% of energy) confers greater mortality risk than moderate intake across multinational cohorts (pooled hazard ratio 1.20, 95% CI 1.09-1.32).
High carbohydrate consumption (>70% of energy) confers greater mortality risk than moderate intake across multinational cohorts (pooled hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.11-1.36).
Substituting animal-derived fat or protein for carbohydrate is associated with an increased risk of overall mortality (pooled hazard ratio 1.18, 95% CI 1.08-1.29).
Substituting plant-derived fat or protein for carbohydrate is associated with a decreased risk of overall mortality (pooled hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.78-0.87).

evidence.description: In the ARIC cohort, after multivariable adjustment, there was a U-shaped association between the percentage of energy consumed from carbohydrate (mean 48.9%, SD 9.4) and mortality.
A percentage of 50-55% energy from carbohydrate was associated with the lowest risk of mortality in the ARIC cohort.
In the meta-analysis of all cohorts (432,179 participants), low carbohydrate consumption (<40%) conferred greater mortality risk than did moderate intake (pooled hazard ratio 1.20, 95% CI 1.09-1.32).
In the meta-analysis of all cohorts, high carbohydrate consumption (>70%) conferred greater mortality risk than did moderate intake (pooled hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.11-1.36).
Mortality increased when carbohydrates were exchanged for animal-derived fat or protein (hazard ratio 1.18, 95% CI 1.08-1.29).
Mortality decreased when carbohydrate substitutions were plant-based (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.78-0.87).

methodologies.name: Prospective cohort study and meta-analysis
methodologies.description: Prospective evaluation of dietary carbohydrate intake and all-cause mortality in the ARIC cohort combined with a meta-analysis of seven multinational prospective studies.
conditions: Exclusion of extreme caloric intake (<600 or >4200 kcal/day for men, <500 or >3600 kcal/day for women)
Median follow-up of 25 years in ARIC cohort
